name: NVIDIA B200
description: The NVIDIA B200 (Blackwell) is the current flagship data-center GPU, built for frontier-scale LLM pre-training with 192GB of HBM3e and a second-generation transformer engine.
highlights: Highest raw training throughput of any card we track — built for trillion-parameter-class models
192GB HBM3e means far less model/pipeline sharding than H100 or H200 pods
Limited early supply keeps prices premium versus Hopper-generation cards

name: NVIDIA H200
description: The NVIDIA H200 keeps the H100's compute but nearly doubles memory (141GB HBM3e) and bandwidth (4.8TB/s), making it the better choice once a model or its KV cache no longer comfortably fits an 80GB card.
highlights: 76% more VRAM and 43% more bandwidth than H100 at the same compute
Drop-in upgrade path from H100 — same Hopper transformer engine and software stack
Serves larger context windows / batch sizes per GPU for LLM inference

name: NVIDIA H100
description: The NVIDIA H100 (Hopper) is the current flagship data-center GPU for large-scale LLM training and fine-tuning, offering a transformer engine with FP8 support and 3.35 TB/s of HBM3 bandwidth.
highlights: Fastest option for multi-billion parameter model training
FP8 transformer engine roughly doubles throughput vs A100
NVLink/NVSwitch scales cleanly to 8x pods for distributed training

name: AMD MI300X
description: AMD's MI300X is the main non-NVIDIA option for large-model serving, pairing 192GB of HBM3 with ROCm software support — a real alternative when H100/H200 capacity is constrained or pricier.
highlights: 192GB VRAM rivals B200/MI300X-class cards at typically lower $/hr than Hopper
Best fit for teams already validated on ROCm/ONNX Runtime rather than pure CUDA
Fewer providers carry it, so availability is more limited than NVIDIA options

name: NVIDIA A100
description: The NVIDIA A100 80GB remains the best price-to-performance workhorse for fine-tuning and mid-size training jobs, with wide availability across every major GPU cloud.
highlights: Best availability-to-price ratio for 7B-70B parameter fine-tuning
80GB VRAM fits most LLM fine-tuning jobs without sharding
Mature software stack, zero compatibility surprises

name: NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada
description: The RTX 6000 Ada is the Ada-generation successor to the RTX A6000: same 48GB workstation-class VRAM, updated architecture and FP8 support, but no NVLink — Ada dropped multi-GPU bridging from the workstation line.
highlights: Newer Ada architecture with FP8 support the Ampere-based RTX A6000 lacks
48GB VRAM at strong single-GPU rendering/inference throughput
Certified drivers for professional DCC/CAD pipelines

name: NVIDIA L40S
description: The L40S is NVIDIA's Ada-generation data-center card built for inference and mixed graphics/AI workloads, offering strong FP8 throughput and 48GB VRAM at a lower price point than H100.
highlights: Purpose-built for inference and generative AI serving at scale
48GB VRAM comfortably serves 13B-34B quantized LLMs
Strong choice when H100 supply is constrained or overkill

name: NVIDIA A40
description: The A40 is Ampere's 48GB data-center rendering/inference card — an older, cheaper alternative to the RTX 6000 Ada with the same VRAM headroom, still common on marketplace clouds.
highlights: 48GB VRAM at a noticeably lower $/hr than newer Ada-generation cards
NVLink bridge support for 2-GPU scaling, unlike its Ada successor
Widely available secondhand/marketplace supply keeps pricing low

name: NVIDIA RTX 5090
description: The RTX 5090 is NVIDIA's newest consumer flagship — 32GB of GDDR7 and a big shader/bandwidth jump over the RTX 4090, currently the fastest consumer card available to rent for image generation and rendering.
highlights: Fastest consumer-class card we track for SDXL/ComfyUI throughput
32GB VRAM — 8GB more than RTX 4090, room for bigger batches or SDXL + ControlNet stacks
Still early in cloud rollout, so supply/pricing is less stable than RTX 4090

name: NVIDIA RTX 4090
description: The RTX 4090 is a consumer-class card that dominates the price-per-token metric for image generation (ComfyUI, Automatic1111, SDXL) and small-model inference thanks to huge shader throughput at a fraction of data-center pricing.
highlights: Cheapest $/hr for Stable Diffusion / ComfyUI workloads
24GB VRAM covers SDXL, most 7B-13B quantized inference
Widely available on spot/marketplace clouds at sub-$0.50/hr

name: NVIDIA RTX A6000
description: The RTX A6000 pairs 48GB of VRAM with workstation-grade drivers, making it a favorite for render farms, CAD/DCC pipelines and mid-size inference workloads that need more headroom than a 4090 without H100 pricing.
highlights: 48GB VRAM handles larger batches than RTX 4090 for the same task class
ECC memory and certified drivers for professional rendering pipelines
Good middle ground between consumer cards and data-center pricing

name: NVIDIA RTX 3090
description: The RTX 3090 is the previous-generation consumer flagship — 24GB of VRAM at the lowest $/hr of any 24GB card on this site, thanks to huge secondhand/marketplace supply on peer-to-peer clouds.
highlights: Lowest cost-per-GB-VRAM of any card we track — hard to beat for budget SDXL/inference
Same 24GB as RTX 4090 at a fraction of the hourly rate, with lower raw throughput
Massive marketplace availability keeps it in stock even during demand spikes

name: NVIDIA V100
description: The V100 is an older data-center card (Volta, 2017) that's still commonly rented for legacy pipelines, teaching/research workloads and budget fine-tuning jobs that don't need Ampere/Hopper-class throughput.
highlights: Cheapest HBM data-center card we track — real memory bandwidth at a fraction of A100 pricing
Still fully supported by CUDA/cuDNN and every major ML framework
Good fit for teaching, small-batch fine-tuning, or reproducing older research

name: NVIDIA A10
description: The A10 is a low-power (150W) inference-focused card — 24GB of VRAM at roughly a third the power draw of an RTX 4090, popular for always-on inference endpoints where electricity cost matters as much as throughput.
highlights: 150W TDP — the lowest power draw of any 24GB card here, cheapest to run 24/7
24GB VRAM comfortably serves most 7B-13B model inference
Data-center-grade reliability without data-center-grade pricing

name: NVIDIA L4
description: The L4 is a single-slot, 72W inference card built for dense, low-power deployment — the cheapest way to run always-on inference or video processing at scale when you don't need training throughput.
highlights: Lowest power draw of any card we track (72W) — very cheap to run continuously
FP8 support despite the low power envelope, unusual for this class of card
Single-slot form factor packs densely into inference-serving racks

name: NVIDIA T4
description: The T4 is the long-running budget inference workhorse of every major cloud — 16GB VRAM, 70W, and the lowest $/hr of any card on this site. Fine for small/quantized models, video transcoding and classic CV pipelines.
highlights: Cheapest card we track — the default choice for cost-sensitive inference at scale
70W TDP and passive-cooling-friendly form factor common in dense inference racks
16GB VRAM is enough for most quantized 7B models or classic CV/video workloads
